A_target.statement:
Let $f$ be [[Definition:Continuous Mapping|continuous]] on a neighborhood of $\tuple {t_0, y_0}$.
Then the [[Definition:Initial Value Problem|initial value problem]]:
:$y' = \map f {t, y}, \quad \map y {t_0} = y_0$
has a solution on some interval $\closedint {t_0 - h} {t_0 + h}$.

B_source.statement:
Let $K$ be a [[Definition:Non-Empty Set|non-empty]] [[Definition:Compact Space|compact]] [[Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)|convex]] subset of a [[Definition:Banach Space|Banach space]] and $T: K \to K$ [[Definition:Continuous Mapping|continuous]].
Then $T$ has a [[Definition:Fixed Point|fixed point]].

substitutions.the compact convex set: a set of uniformly bounded, equicontinuous functions on a small interval
substitutions.the continuous self-map: the integral operator sending y to the integral of f along y
substitutions.a fixed point of the operator: a solution of the differential equation

derived.the fixed point equation: the integral equation equivalent to the initial value problem
derived.existence without uniqueness: solutions need not be unique, since continuity alone is assumed

object_map.reformulation: Convert the differential equation into an integral equation so that solving it becomes finding a fixed point of an operator.

validity_conditions: The initial value problem is equivalent to an integral equation, whose solutions are exactly the fixed points of the integral operator.
The operator maps a suitable ball into a set of uniformly bounded equicontinuous functions, which is relatively compact by Arzela-Ascoli; this supplies the compactness Schauder requires.
Only continuity of f is assumed, so uniqueness fails in general; obtaining uniqueness requires a Lipschitz condition and a contraction argument instead.
proof_plan:
The initial value problem is equivalent to the integral equation:
:$\displaystyle \map y t = y_0 + \int_{t_0}^t \map f {s, \map y s} \rd s$

Define on $\map C {\closedint {t_0 - h} {t_0 + h} }$:
:$\displaystyle \map {\paren {T y} } t = y_0 + \int_{t_0}^t \map f {s, \map y s} \rd s$
whose fixed points are the solutions.

Let $\size f \le M$ near $\tuple {t_0, y_0}$, and let $K$ be the closed convex set of $y$ with $\size {y - y_0} \le b$, where $M h \le b$.
Then $T$ maps $K$ into itself, and $\map T K$ is [[Definition:Equicontinuous|equicontinuous]] with Lipschitz constant $M$.
By the [[Arzelà-Ascoli Theorem]], $\map T K$ is relatively compact.
